title: Mass Number (A) & Isotopes
topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Mass number:** the sum of masses of sub-atomic particles contained in an atom is responsible for the mass of that atom. Since the mass of electrons is negligible, the mass of an atom is the sum of the masses of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus; the mass of an atom is concentrated on the nucleus.
**Whole number:** a mass number is a whole number since the number of protons and neutrons are whole numbers; it is generally denoted with the letter A.

**Notation:** the mass number is written as a superscript to the symbol of the element; for an atom (X) whose atomic number is Z and mass number is A, the symbol is written with Z as a subscript and A as a superscript.
**Formulas:** Mass number (A) = atomic number (Z) + number of neutrons (N); A = Z + N; A = pâº + nâ°; Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons.

**Isotopes definition:** in 1919, F.W. Aston found that certain elements consist of two or more types of atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, which are called isotopes. The word isotope (coined by Soddy in 1913) comes from two Latin words, isos = the same and topos = position/place.

**Isotope properties:** isotopes are different atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different atomic masses; they possess the same position in the modern periodic table, have the same number of protons and electrons but a different number of neutrons, and possess identical chemical properties (due to same atomic number) but different physical properties (due to different mass numbers).

**Abundance:** around 1000 isotopes have been identified, of which nearly 300 are stable and occur in nature; the stability and natural abundance of isotopes differ. Chlorine has two isotopes, whereas krypton has nearly 20 isotopes. Most abundant isotopes occur from 90-99% with respect to other isotopes, but Cl-35 occurs 75% compared to Cl-37 (25%) in nature.
